# Top 5 posts from r/MovieSuggestions day

## 1. Looking for a film with a good twist even I can't predict.

**Score:** 75

It doesn't ruin my enjoyment of watching, though I do want to look for series or films that are a little less predictable, that pose a challenge to predict  and speculate along.

I have access to Netflix, Prime, HBO and Disney+. I'm interested in most genres, except horror or excessively pornographic (sex scenes are fine, just not if it's the majority of the thing).

  
ETA: I'd like relatively new / recent things (\~5 years old).

## 2. It's Noirvember!

**Score:** 30
**Body:** It's Noirvember, and I'm looking to explore more film noir!

Some of my favourites are **M (1931), Sunset Boulevard (1950), The Night of the Hunter (1955), and The Third Man (1949)**.

I'm looking for films with a similar atmosphere, strong visual style, interesting characters, psychological tension, and perhaps a dark or unsettling undertone.

I'm open to both classic film noir and neo-noir.

What would you recommend? What are your personal favourites?

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. The Maltese Falcon is the gold standard.  Chinatown is also great (but it's in color). Heck, I would even consider Who Framed Roger Rabbit.
  - I wouldnt have immediately thought of Who Framed Roger Rabbit, but honestly it does have a noir feel to it. The setting and the whole mystery work surprisingly well together. Now I want to rewatch it.
2. Classic noir: Sweet Smell of Success, Lady from Shanghai and The Cat People are my three top classics. I’m assuming you’ve seen Double Indemnity but maybe I shouldn’t, if you haven’t seen it you definitely should check it out!

Miami neo-noir is a whole world from the 80s,  Body Heat and Miami Blues are both fabulous.

For modern, I love Bound, absolutely incredible film, so tense, and of course Brick. The Lookout is a fabulous movie I don’t see talked about much, I found it because Roger Ebert fell in love with it. I also loved Thoroughbreds, which I seldom see recommended, probably because it is candy-colored noir, but it definitely qualifies. The question is which one of them is the femme fatale… Anton Yelchin’s last film.
3. Check out Dead Men Don’t Wear Plaid starring Steve Martin. It’s a brilliant movie that uses clips from classic Noir films and new Black and White footage to make a whole new movie plot they makes sense. It’s hilarious. 
4. In a lonely place

Touch of evil
5. Chinatown (1974)

Farewell, My Lovely (1975)

Kiss Me Deadly (1955)

Laura (1944)

The Maltese Falcon (1941)

Nightmare Alley (1947)

[https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/devil\_in\_a\_blue\_dress](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/devil_in_a_blue_dress)

## 2. I've spent the past 3 days watching the Peter Jackson trilogy for the first time.

**Score:** 193
**Body:** I can't believe it's taken me this long to start watching the Lord of the Rings films. For 23 years of my life, the only fantasy I consumed was Harry Potter, but I have discovered the wonders of franchises like Avatar: The Last Airbender and, of course, Lord of the Rings. I didn't know what I was missing until I watched it. I'm glad to now finally have watched The Lord of the Rings films, as they are a beautifully shot, perfectly acted, brilliantly scored cinematic masterpiece. The only trilogy that comes close is Back to the Future. It amazes me that each film was filmed at the exact same time and released each year from 2001 to 2003. If Tolken had lived to see these films he would be amazed. I might need to start reading the books, as if the films are this great, then the books must be just as good if not better.

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Imagine watching Bad Taste and Brain Dead and going, yeah, let's do the most expensive trilogy to date on one of the most beloved stories with this director.  It's a stunning achievement 
  - Only in our universe would that have been a good idea
  - <comes up from the third gram of coke while watching *Meet the Feebles*\>

“GET ME PETER JACKSON! THE MAN NEEDS TO MAKE THE FUCKING LORD OF THE RINGS!”
2. Watch the extended versions. They a super long and you should take an intermission but better then the theatrical release 
3. Yea, it's the best thing ever. Seeing them in theaters when they first came out was a feeling like no other. Hair-raising is the best word for it. We had never seen fantasy creatures and places look so real. Doing Fellowship basically as a horror movie is still one of the coolest decisions I've ever seen in a movie adaptation. There is so much creativity and filmmaking craft in every minute of those movies, I think of them as being in some ways the pinnacle of moviemaking. Just the sheer work of so many people and so many jobs well done. Every technique and trick in existence was brought to bear.

The cast is beyond lightning in a bottle. I think if you could have selected from any actor who has ever lived, you'd still end up with like 90% of the same cast. They were simply the correct people to play those characters. Who better than Sean Bean to play Boromir, like ever? He was made for that character. Ian McKellen, I mean come on. Christopher Lee. John Rhys-Davies. Viggo Mortensen. It's insane that they were all at the exact right age and stage of their careers for these movies. 
  - Definitely a formative cinematic experience for me as a high schooler. Walking out of the theater after ROTK remains etched in my memory.
4. Glad I got to watch these when they premiered in theaters.
5. I agree, they are excellent movies.

Watched them countless times. I watch them atleast once a year around christmas/new years and then maybe also once od twice during the year.


6. I might have spent 200/250 hours watching the trilogy over and over, for the last 20 years, and I still consider it was time very well spent.
7. My personal take is that the LOTR is the greatest film accomplishment of all time.

Edit - at least this generation

## 3. does anyone know what Beyond the Black Rainbow is even about?

**Score:** 129
**Body:** a truly gorgeous movie, probably one of my favorite soundtracks of all time. but my god it felt like i was eating the tastiest nothing burger i’ve ever had, for most of it. the pacing is incredibly slow, and the story was very confusing to me, would love some help to understand it.   
I love Cosmatos’ Mandy but struggled a lot more to sit through this one. 

### Top 9 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Yes. I will not elaborate unless we are smoking a joint together.
  - The appropriate ritual to approach to Panos Cosmatos discourse with full efficacy.
2. The idea behind the movie was that this was a throwback to late-70s concepts of psychedelia leading to the evolution of the human mind. This whole underground company was, in theory, a cutting-edge research lab where that's exactly what they did. But the guy who currently runs it, having once been a test subject himself, has been driven psychotic by what he took and is holding the one girl hostage. As a point of fascination, she's everything he wishes he had become, and he kind of resents her for it as well as idolises her for it.

Both main characters are rarely fully conscious. They're both in a haze of psychedelic delirium at all times, and the movie follows that pace. It's almost as if everything we're seeing is heavily tainted by dream logic because the place was constructed by people who were living in waking dream logic and are currently experiencing a half-sleep state of mind. 

I could go on, but that's the basics. 
3. Yeah, it’s about being fucking awesome while vibing to an amazing soundtrack.

There's other subtext that isn't too subtle, like criticism of religion, the patriarchy, confronting grief. But it's mostly a style movie, and imho a really fucking good one with a stellar soundtrack.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. You Can See Everything is a movie about Trump and the Trump-age of America

**Score:** 74
**Body:** I think the readings of this movie as a work about epistemology or a perverse hitchcokian romance are really fascinating. But i also think people are overlooking how apt this movie is as a definitive reflection on the past ten years. 

Trump is THE master manipulator. Everything he says is a lie. He has no past times or pleasures or interests in art. Just an unceasing desire to acquire power and manipulate others for the sake of manipulation itself. And his aesthetic of dishonesty has bled out into mainstream american culture in all sorts of ways. In America today, dishonesty is in the air we breathe. 

For instance, how Billy and Elizabeth operate in the “training montage” sequence where they make a ton of calls and just bullshit sell all of these nonsense ideas. Or later, when Nathan tries to interview the tech guy. There’s an undercurrent to this movie that reflects on how fraudulent the tech economy is today. And other themes connecting that to the rise of the alt right. 

In total, I think the movie captures this overall aesthetic that is everywhere, and so definitive of the modern day, where everything looks and feels like Elizabeth Holmes. Just aggressively bullshitting you. Wide eyed and shameless. And so unperturbed by the immorality of their actions, morality ceases to be a thing. 

### Top 5 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Both Billy and Trump exist in their current forms because of the systems that rewarded their lies and manipulations with industrial and political success. None of these people are very interesting, deep, or particularly special, they are just ordinary human beings hollowed out by unregulated late stage capitalism. They, and the points of the movie you highlight, are reflections of that system more than of each other. 
  - Going to see this movie this weekend so no spoilers (I know I shouldn't be here but I could resist!)

I read Bad Blood as a build up for this documentary because I knew her name and Theranos but not much else. After learning all of the shit she was actually found guilty of it's wild to see the redemption arc she is having online from the movie.
    - The "redemption arc" will make more sense to you once you see the movie, and consider that most people don't know what you know about her.
    - It’s a great movie and even better if you know as little as possible. I made a bad choice and clicked on some posts about the movie and had some small things spoiled. Don’t be me lol!
2. It's about the "post-truth" era in general: Trump, alternative media, the end of journalism, billionaires buying their own PR...it is certainly a film about our current era. I think it will be considered one of the (if not THE) defining film of the 2020s
3. I wish Nathan would have exposed more of Holmes' lies. His "who's on first" schtick and the scene where she says she never told a lie only scratched the surface of her pathology. After leaving the cinema many people seemed to think she was some sort of victim without agency while the evil men in her life manipulated her, which is ridiculous.
  - The movie wasn’t about Holmes and whether or not she was guilty though. All of that stuff is already out there. It seems like the people making that criticism are missing the point of what they are watching. 
    - completely agree,   those 2 nutjobs sociopaths are just a tool
  - I didn’t get that at all. For me, the closing moments of the film sewed just enough doubt to make me think Holmes was far more sinister than the act she put on 
4. i dont necessarily agree with your analysis but i agree with your overall statement. the fact that people with access to the highest amounts of wealth and power are as insane, detached from reality, and willing to lie to the extent that the holmes couple are was all over the movie. i dont even mean just in how billy interacts with elizabeth, but in how they dealt w the a24 producers, how they sockpuppet elizabeth's account to boost AI, like this is how deals are made in this age and to me that was really the most striking part of the movie

## 2. Bicycle Thieves (1948) - Indeed, A Timeless Masterpiece

**Score:** 29
**Body:** Finally got around to see this for the first time, and it is indeed a timeless masterpiece. 

I would suggest the film is not as simple as it seems, with their definitely being a strong artistic sensibility behind it, the film being quite poetic at times. I found this to be a surprise considering this was one of the first neo-realist films in Italy. 

It's visually stunning, superbly written, and incredibly intimate. A story like this one works in my opinion because we are able to gain access to the interiority of Antonio, and to a lesser extent, his boy, Bruno.

It has the feeling of a classic hollywood movie, but I suppose the revoluntinary thing about this movie at the time, and something we take for granted now, is the lead is just an ordinary man. I could see this being one of the first to change how movies were viewed in italy, and perhaps around the world, of them being not mere vessels for escapism, but artistic creations that had the capability to reveal truths about human nature and society.

I'd imagine it's a film that a war-ravaged Italy needed at the time, a film to humanise the many struggling people of it's country and really show what the conditions were doing to them.

The ending is incredibly simple, not a large ordeal, but ultimately gut-wrenching and tragic, putting a dephiant full-stop to the film. I noticed Antonio becomes more and more a character who is slightly detatched from the audience, which I interpret as us taking the gaze of Bruno as the film nears the end, and seeing not Anotonio as simply a worker in Italy trying to find his bicycle, but as a dad trying to maintain his dignity for his son. We all have fathers, so this is incredibly relateable and painful.

Another thing that I took away was, the children of these fathers, being brought up in these desperate post-war conditions, inheriting the economic anxieties of their parents, seeing the loss of dignity they had to endure, and the inability of religion in making any material impact. How this shaped the post-war generation and explained the character of nation after that point.

Religion is really an afterthought in this movie, there's no praying, no counselling, just a man deseperate to find the key to his family's sustenance. There's a great irony of him only ending up in a place of worship to confront a man who he believes played a part in the theft. And another greater irony, of him as a last resort, seeking counsel from a fortune-teller.

I haven't seen a better, or more powerful film than this one, in showing what dire times can do to the dignity of a human being. 

Strongly recommend watching this one on the big screen if ever given the chance. It sneaks up on you in the end, and is certain to have a devestating impact, but also rejuvenating in a weird way, because of the great piece of art it is.

### Top 1 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. As someone with Italian heritage, I really appreciate that the English title of the film is now referred to as “Bicycle Thieves” *plural,* and not “The Bicycle Thief”, which is was known as for decades.

Because so central to the film is not only that Antonio himself becomes a bicycle thief (meaning that the story has more than one), but that really the film is a portrait of a desperate, post-WW2 Italy, where work is in short supply and anyone can become a common thief because they have no other choice.

My father was born in Italy around the time this film was made, and his family moved to Australia in 1955 because things in the south of the country were so desperate.

What makes this film so resonant to me is that it really gives an insight into a society on the brink… something that is increasingly relevant again in this time, sadly.

## 3. Can a film help us understand our own lives better than a direct conversation about them?

**Score:** 22
**Body:** I've been a filmmaker for more than 25 years, and one of the most fascinating things I've discovered is that sometimes people find it easier to talk about a fictional character's struggles than their own.

For example, I've spent considerable time exploring *The Shawshank Redemption* with groups of adults. Ask someone directly about their relationship with hope, despair, or regret, and you might get a guarded response. But ask them whether Red was truly a free man when he left prison, and suddenly they're talking about freedom, identity, institutionalization, and the ghosts of their own past.

I've seen similar things happen with *Stand By Me*, where discussions about Gordie, Chris, and the loss of childhood become conversations about friendship, family, grief, and the people we might have become.

I've developed a program called Cinema Therapy through my PhD program (Interdisciplinary Health Sciences) that uses film, improvisation, and creative writing to explore these connections.  A*esthetic distance* has become the secret sauce in this work. It generally defines the space between ourselves and a work of art that allows us to engage with difficult emotions without confronting them quite so directly.

When I've found myself saying "I see myself in (X character),"  I'm often discovering something about myself - something I've often thought was "just me." 

I'm curious how others here think about this, particularly with films that have changed meaning for you as you've grown older.

**Have you ever returned to a film and realized that the characters hadn't changed—but you had? And maybe seen something that is quite obvious to you now, but flew by you in previous viewings?**

### Top 4 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. For me cinema has primarily been a way of understanding other people, and especially other cultures.  I first began watching world cinema as a teenager in my pretty dead end hometown, where I didn't feel like I would ever have much chance of traveling and meeting a lot of different people.  (In the end I wasn't wrong, despite a few trips I cherish travel is really expensive for normal people haha).  I have rarely thought of cinema as a way of understanding myself better, though of course the act of empathy might intrinsically be that as well.
2. Growing up I basically learned how to be a person by watching films. I'm not diagnosed but, 38 years old now, I'm pretty sure I'm either AdHD or autistic, or a bit of both, and was especially burdened as a kid and adolescent with social anxiety and feelings of being an outsider. Didn't have many friends and didn't go out much, spent most of my free time watching films, analyzing characters, thinking about how I related to them, and took notes on the many ways their (my) ways of thinking led down dark paths. I was pretty into Scorsese's films and connected with the masculine alienation, insecurities around women, and seeing the self-destruction of those characters was one of the things that pushed me out of my isolation and into a healthier dynamic with others. Took a very long time to feel healthy, happy and confident, and it wasn't just film that got me there, but it played a big part. Regarding your specific question- I really loved the movie Ghost World as a teenager, I thought those girls were so cool the way they cut everyone down. Not so much anymore... Still love the film though.
3. Narrative bypasses a lot of filters. Narrative that runs contrary to our assumptions is compelling and inviting. Facts that run contrary to our assumptions are dangerous and scary. There’s a reason why politicians use narratives. Even when they cite facts they’re still building and spreading narratives. Narratives are also easier to grok and remember. While the facts of an experience or a story might fade and shift, the underlying narrative stays crystal clear. There’s a cool saying I heard recently that’s “war is fought with bullets, peace is fought with stories.”

I don’t really have any experience I can remember of my perspective shifting around a story as I changed or as I grew up. At most I’ve had a “wow this didn’t age well”
  - that quote (which I like, too) maybe it's: "Wars are fought with guns. The peace is fought with stories." - from [***American War***](https://www.google.com/search?kgmid=%2Fg%2F11g8w90jvl&q=American+War) by Egyptian-Canadian author and journalist Omar El Akkad?
    - Oh yeah that’s the one
4. Your studies are so fucking cool! 

I've absolutely witnessed the phenomena you have both professionally (I'm a therapist) and personally. I think that's one of the great powers of art, and an inconvenient truth for all the folks out there who think people can challenge and confront others into reflection: People tend to learn best when they feel safe, not on the defensive. That's why 

Books like *White Fragility* did not change the world and mostly pissed people off

but I watched *Amistad* recently

and was more impacted by its horrific depiction of enslaved Africans than by any woke-y book or culturally competent counselors class I've ever taken.

I constantly return to narratives and find I've changed based on my reaction to the characters. It's one of my favorite reasons for rewatching movies. I'm on a 100-new-to-me-movies quest for 2026 and really miss rewatching.




## 4. When Does Cinematic Inspiration Become Imitation? Rethinking Originality Through Bollywood film "King"

**Score:** 7
**Body:** I recently posted about *King*, the upcoming Bollywood film directed by Siddharth Anand, and the discussion around cinematic similarities ended up being more interesting to me than the original comparison itself.

Some of the comments made me think about a broader question that goes beyond *King*:

When does cinematic inspiration become imitation?

We can look at a burning house, an extreme close-up, a particular composition, an action sequence, or even a familiar character dynamic and immediately recognize another film.

But recognition isn't necessarily proof of copying.

Filmmakers don't create in isolation. They grow up watching other films. Visual grammar travels across generations, countries, genres and industries. Hollywood influences Bollywood. Bollywood influences other film industries. Korean cinema influences Hollywood. French cinema influences American filmmakers. And sometimes two filmmakers simply arrive at similar images because cinema has developed a shared visual vocabulary.

That makes me wonder whether we sometimes judge the *same cinematic behavior differently depending on who is doing it*.

When a filmmaker we already regard as an auteur references another film, we might call it homage, intertextuality or cinematic conversation.

When a filmmaker or industry we perceive as less prestigious uses a similar image, are we quicker to call it derivative?

That question became particularly interesting to me with *King*. There are already discussions around Siddharth Anand's relationship with Hollywood-style action filmmaking and whether his visual language feels familiar. Some viewers see that familiarity as evidence that he lacks originality; others see it as part of the language of contemporary commercial action cinema.

I'm not interested in deciding that debate for everyone.

I'd rather ask:

What actually separates influence from imitation?

Is it the similarity of the image?

The intention behind it?

What the filmmaker does with the image afterward?

Or does originality require us to create visual language that has never existed before?

And perhaps there is another question underneath all of this:

Do we sometimes confuse “I recognize where this came from” with “there is nothing original happening here”?

I'd genuinely love to hear how cinephiles think about this… when comparing filmmaking traditions across Bollywood, Hollywood and other world cinemas.

Because maybe cinema isn't a collection of completely original ideas.

Maybe it's an ongoing conversation where every generation borrows, transforms, challenges and reinterprets what came before.

And *King* just happens to be an interesting place to have that conversation.
